edges.description: Mutant SAMD9L, both truncating and ATXPC missense alleles, represses protein synthesis more strongly than wild type at the same expression level.

The neurologic disease follows from the constitutional variant in neural tissue rather than from the hematopoietic lesion: it persists when blood has been rescued and progresses after transplantation. The intermediate mechanism in neurons is unresolved.
Interferon raises expression of the truncated SAAD protein, which then suppresses global protein synthesis.
The translation block is proposed to account for the lineage-dominant failure of hematopoietic progenitors and lymphocytes; the authors frame the lineage specificity as a sensitivity difference.

nodes.description: Copy-neutral loss of heterozygosity of 7q (uniparental disomy) that retains only the wild-type allele, or an acquired truncating SAMD9L variant in cis with the germline variant, restores hematopoiesis without loss of chromosome 7. Revertant clones are associated with hematologic remission and milder disease, and can make a carrier appear unaffected. This is a protective terminal branch: it has no phenotype target because its consequence is the absence of cytopenia.

nodes.description: Slowly progressive cerebellar degeneration with Purkinje-cell involvement, sensorimotor axonal neuropathy and cerebral white matter change. Neurologic onset is typically in adolescence or adulthood, later than the hematologic disease, and imaging changes can precede symptoms. In the SCA49 family SAMD9L localized to mitochondria and patient fibroblasts showed mitochondrial perturbation; in one SAAD infant autopsy showed selective Purkinje-cell loss. How SAMD9L variants damage neurons is unresolved.

nodes.description: No established guideline exists. GeneReviews suggests hematology review and CBC every 6-12 months, baseline and annual marrow examination by shared decision, more frequent monitoring for new cytopenias or monosomy 7, and annual immunologic evaluation.
